title: Tuning for Software Analytics: is it Really Necessary?

edges.target: Differential evolution (Storn & Price)
edges.ref: [12] R. Storn, K. Price, Differential evolution-a simple and efficient heuristic for global optimization over continuous spaces, J. Global Optimization 11(4) (1997) 341-359
edges.evidence: we ran differential evolution as an optimizer to explore the tuning space (as a first step) then tested the tunings using hold-out data

edges.target: Storn's population-size recommendation (np = 10x attributes)
edges.ref: [12] R. Storn, K. Price, Differential evolution-a simple and efficient heuristic for global optimization over continuous spaces, J. Global Optimization 11(4) (1997) 341-359
edges.evidence: Rainer Storn (one of the inventors of DE) recommends setting np to be ten times larger than the number of attributes being optimized [12]. ... no evidence that np = 10 is a poor choice

edges.target: Lessmann et al. benchmark of 22 learners (RF best, CART worst)
edges.ref: [4] S. Lessmann, B. Baesens, C. Mues, S. Pietsch, Benchmarking classification models for software defect prediction, IEEE TSE 34(4) (2008) 485-496
edges.evidence: this paper shows we can refute the conclusions of Lessmann et al. in the sense that, after tuning, CART performs just as well as Random Forest

edges.target: Hall et al. SLR (simple learners such as LR beat Random Forest)
edges.ref: [5] T. Hall, S. Beecham, D. Bowes, D. Gray, S. Counsell, A systematic review of fault prediction performance in software engineering, IEEE TSE 38(6) (2012) 1276-1304
edges.evidence: LR will be used, untuned, in order to check one of the recommendations made by Hall et al. [5]. ... tuning raises doubts about the optimality of the Hall et al. recommendation

edges.target: Lessmann et al. grid-search tuning protocol
edges.ref: [4] S. Lessmann, B. Baesens, C. Mues, S. Pietsch, Benchmarking classification models for software defect prediction, IEEE TSE 34(4) (2008) 485-496
edges.evidence: Lessmann et al.[4] tuned parameters for some of their algorithms using a grid search ... This is a slow approach

edges.target: PROMISE defect data (ant, camel, ivy, jedit, log4j, lucene, poi, synapse, velocity, xerces)
edges.ref: [1] T. Menzies, C. Pape, M. Rees-Jones, The promise repository of empirical software engineering data (Feb 2015). URL http://openscience.us/repo
edges.evidence: Our defect data comes from the PROMISE repository (http://openscience.us/repo/defect) and pertains to open source Java systems defined in terms of Table 1

edges.target: Scikit-learn (CART, Random Forest, LR implementations)
edges.ref: [38] F. Pedregosa et al., Scikit-learn: Machine learning in Python, Journal of Machine Learning Research 12 (2011) 2825-2830
edges.evidence: For this study, we use CART, Random Forest and LR versions from SciKitLearn [38]

edges.target: WHERE learner (Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [37] T. Menzies, A. Butcher, D. Cok, A. Marcus, L. Layman, F. Shull, B. Turhan, T. Zimmermann, Local versus global lessons for defect prediction and effort estimation, IEEE TSE 39(6) (2013) 822-834
edges.evidence: WHERE, which is available from github.com/ai-se/where. ... this paper uses WHERE since, as shown below, it offers an interesting case study on the benefits of tuning

edges.target: CART (Breiman et al.)
edges.ref: [36] L. Breiman, J. H. Friedman, R. A. Olshen, C. J. Stone, Classification and Regression Trees, 1984
edges.evidence: There are several ways to make defect predictors using CART [35], Random Forest [36], WHERE [37] and LR

edges.target: Random Forest (Breiman & Cutler)
edges.ref: [35] L. Breiman, A. Cutler, Random forests, https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/RandomForests (2001)
edges.evidence: Random Forest divides data like CART then builds F > 1 trees, each time using some random subset of the attributes

edges.target: Fayyad-Irani discretizer / InfoGain (inside WHERE)
edges.ref: [41] U. M. Fayyad, I. H. Irani, Multi-interval discretization of continuous-valued attributes for classification learning, IJCAI 1993, pp. 1022-1027
edges.evidence: WHERE pretends its clusters are "classes", then asks the InfoGain algorithm of the Fayyad-Irani discretizer [41], to rank the attributes

edges.target: Principal component analysis (Jolliffe), as WHERE's projection
edges.ref: [40] I. Jolliffe, Principal component analysis, Wiley Online Library, 2002
edges.evidence: WHERE projects the data on to a dimension it synthesizes from the raw data using a process analogous to principle component analysis [40]

edges.target: Menzies, Greenwald & Frank 2007 (NASA defect predictors, off-the-shelf tunings, grid search takes days)
edges.ref: [15] T. Menzies, J. Greenwald, A. Frank, Data mining static code attributes to learn defect predictors, IEEE TSE 33(1) (2007) 2-13
edges.evidence: we have explored grid search for defect prediction and found it takes days to terminate [15]. ... Defect predictors often find the location of 70% (or more) of the defects in code [15]

edges.target: Menzies, Greenwald & Frank 2007 (learner rankings with default tunings)
edges.ref: [15] T. Menzies, J. Greenwald, A. Frank, Data mining static code attributes to learn defect predictors, IEEE TSE 33(1) (2007) 2-13
edges.evidence: Tuning changes conclusions on what learners are better than others. Hence, it is time to revisit numerous prior publications of our own [15] and others [4, 5]

edges.target: Menzies & Di Stefano 2003 (success/failure factors in software reuse)
edges.ref: [8] T. Menzies, J. D. Stefano, More success and failure factors in software reuse, IEEE TSE 29(5) (2003) 474-477
edges.evidence: one of us (Menzies) used data miners to assert that some factors were more important than others ... That assertion should now be doubted since Menzies did not conduct a tuning study

edges.target: Menzies et al. 'Sharing Data and Models' (advice: do not tune, too hard)
edges.ref: [39] T. Menzies, E. Kocaguneli, L. Minku, F. Peters, B. Turhan, Sharing Data and Models in Software Engineering, Morgan Kaufmann, 2015
edges.evidence: many researchers in this field were content to take our prior advice of "do not tune... it is just too hard" [39]

edges.target: Prior SBSE evolutionary-optimizer work (Feather/Menzies, Krall GALE, Green et al.) expecting thousands of evaluations
edges.ref: [44,45,52,60,61] e.g. J. Krall, T. Menzies, M. Davies, Gale: Geometric active learning for search-based software engineering, IEEE TSE; P. Green II, T. Menzies et al., ASE'09
edges.evidence: our expectations were that non-parametric evolutionary optimization would take thousands, if not millions, of evaluations of candidate tunings. This turned out not to be that case

edges.target: Bergstra & Bengio, random search for hyper-parameter optimization
edges.ref: [13] J. Bergstra, Y. Bengio, Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization, Journal of Machine Learning Research 13 (2012) 281-305
edges.evidence: Bergstra and Bengio [13] comment that for most data sets only a few of the tuning parameters really matter ... the important tunings are different for different data sets

edges.target: Baker PhD thesis (grid search misses optimizations)
edges.ref: [21] D. Baker, A Hybrid Approach to Expert and Model-based Effort Estimation, Ph.D. thesis, West Virginia University (2007)
edges.evidence: Not only that, we found that grid search can miss important optimizations [21]

edges.target: Vesterstrom & Thomsen (DE competitive with PSO and GAs)
edges.ref: [54] J. Vesterstrom, R. Thomsen, A comparative study of differential evolution, particle swarm optimization, and evolutionary algorithms on numerical benchmark problems, CEC'04
edges.evidence: Vesterstrom and Thomsen [54] found DE to be competitive with particle swarm optimization and other GAs

edges.target: Cohen: compare against simplest alternative; Holte: simple 'scout' learners
edges.ref: [42] P. R. Cohen, Empirical Methods for Artificial Intelligence, MIT Press, 1995; [43] R. Holte, Very simple classification rules perform well..., Machine Learning 11 (1993) 63
edges.evidence: Cohen [42] advises comparing new methods against the simplest possible alternative. Similarly, Holte [43] recommends using very simple learners as a kind of "scout"

edges.target: Rahman et al. ICSE'14 (static bug finders vs statistical defect prediction equivalent)
edges.ref: [34] F. Rahman, S. Khatri, E. Barr, P. Devanbu, Comparing static bug finders and statistical prediction, ICSE 2014, pp. 424-434
edges.evidence: They found no significant differences in the cost-effectiveness of these approaches. Given this equivalence, it is significant to note that static code defect prediction can be quickly adapted

edges.target: IEEE Metrics 2002 panel / Fagan inspections (manual review defect-detection rates)
edges.ref: [32] F. Shull, V. Basili, B. Boehm et al., What we have learned about fighting defects, IEEE Metrics 2002, pp. 249-258; [33] M. Fagan, IBM Systems Journal 15(3)
edges.evidence: a panel at IEEE Metrics 2002 [32] concluded that manual software reviews can find ~60% of defects ... around 50% for full Fagan inspections [33] to 21%

edges.target: Nagappan & Ball (static attributes automatically collectable)
edges.ref: [3] N. Nagappan, T. Ball, Static analysis tools as early indicators of pre-release defect density, ICSE '05, ACM, 2005, pp. 580-586
edges.evidence: Static code attributes can be automatically collected, even for very large systems [3]

not_reuse_examples: [16] Elish & Elish SVM study: only discussed as an example from the 50-paper literature sample that did no tuning; not run or compared against.
[22-26] Anda/Arisholm/Ostrand/Rahman/Yin: cited only to illustrate that different projects optimize different goals; none of their measures are used.
[55,56] Omran et al., Chiha et al.: cited as prior applications of DE for tuning; background only. Likewise [62] Furnkranz and [63] hyper-heuristics are future-work musings.
Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, precision/recall/F: used but with no citation (textbook), so no statmethod edge per rubric.
notes: Empirical SBSE/defect-prediction paper (arXiv 2016, Fu/Menzies/Shen) tuning CART/RF/WHERE via DE on PROMISE Java data; strong refutes polarity toward Lessmann, Hall, Storn's np rule and several of Menzies' own prior papers; the KS test is uncited so not typed statmethod.
